subject: math
title: Money: Canadian Coins and Bills to 200¢ and $200
seo_title: Grade 2 Money Worksheets: Canadian Coins and Bills, Free with Answer Key (Ontario)
standard_text: Identify different ways of representing the same amount of money up to 200¢ using various combinations of Canadian coins, and up to $200 using $1 and $2 coins and $5, $10, $20, $50, and $100 bills
meta_desc: Free Grade 2 math worksheets on money for the Ontario curriculum: name Canadian coins and bills, count nickels, dimes, quarters, loonies and toonies to 200¢, count bills to $200, make the same amount in different ways and use the fewest coins. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Count money by value, not by the number of coins.
key_sub: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢, 65¢. A quarter is 25¢, not 20¢. The same amount can be made in many ways: 2 quarters = 5 dimes = 50¢.
body_html:
Canadian coins and bills

Learn the name and the value of each coin. Size does not tell you the value. The dime is the smallest coin, but it is worth more than the nickel.

CoinValueGood to know
nickel5¢2 nickels = 1 dime
dime10¢10 dimes = 100¢
quarter25¢4 quarters = 100¢
loonie$1 = 100¢11 sides, gold colour
toonie$2 = 200¢2 loonies = 1 toonie

Count the money, biggest first

Put the coins in order, biggest value first. Then count on.

Example

Count a loonie, 2 quarters and 1 dime.

100¢, then 125¢, 150¢, then 160¢.

Answer: 160¢

Example

Count a $20 bill, a $5 bill and 2 toonies.

$20, then $25, then $27, $29.

Answer: $29

The same amount in different ways

50¢ can be 2 quarters, or 5 dimes, or 1 quarter, 2 dimes and 1 nickel. $10 can be a $10 bill, 2 $5 bills or 5 toonies.

For the fewest coins, use the biggest coin you can each time. 30¢ is 1 quarter and 1 nickel: only 2 coins.

Example

Show 75¢ in two ways.

3 quarters: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢. Or 7 dimes and 1 nickel: 70¢, 75¢.

Answer: 3 quarters, or 7 dimes and 1 nickel

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
4 coins, so 4¢Count the value of each coin: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢, 65¢
A quarter is 20¢A quarter is 25¢. Four quarters make 100¢
The nickel is bigger, so it is worth moreThe small dime is 10¢. The nickel is 5¢
A toonie is $1A loonie is $1. A toonie is $2
Start with the small coinsStart with the biggest coin, then count on

faq.q: What do Grade 2 students learn about money in Ontario?
faq.a: In the Ontario math curriculum (Financial Literacy, F1.1), Grade 2 students show the same amount of money in different ways: up to 200¢ with Canadian coins, and up to $200 with loonies, toonies and $5, $10, $20, $50 and $100 bills.

faq.q: How do I help my child count coins?
faq.a: Sort the coins and start with the biggest value, then count on: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢, 65¢. Use real coins at home and say the value of each one, not just the number of coins.

faq.q: Why are there no pennies in Canada?
faq.a: Canada stopped giving out pennies in 2013. Cash totals are rounded to the nearest 5¢, so the nickel is the smallest coin children count.

Not yet. Making change for simple cash purchases starts in Grade 3. In Grade 2, children count money, make the same amount in different ways and solve simple adding and subtracting problems with money.

items.q: Which coin is worth more?

items.q: Which coin is worth the least?

items.e: A toonie is $2. The bill is $5. $5 is more than $2, so the $5 bill is worth more.

items.q: How many nickels make a dime?
items.e: A nickel is 5¢. 5¢ + 5¢ = 10¢. So 2 nickels make a dime.

items.q: How many nickels make a quarter?
items.e: Count by 5s: 5¢, 10¢, 15¢, 20¢, 25¢. That is 5 nickels. 4 nickels make only 20¢.

items.q: How many quarters make 100¢?
items.e: Count by 25s: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢. That is 4 quarters. 5 is right only if a quarter were 20¢.

items.q: How many dimes make 100¢?
items.e: Count by 10s: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢ … 100¢. That is 10 dimes.

items.q: How many loonies make a toonie?
items.e: A loonie is $1. A toonie is $2. $1 + $1 = $2, so 2 loonies make a toonie.

items.q: How many $10 bills make $100?
items.e: Count by 10s: $10, $20, $30 … $100. That is 10 bills.

items.q: How much money is this?
items.e: Each dime is 10¢. Count by 10¢: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢, 40¢. That is 40¢. Count the value of each coin, not the number of coins. 4¢ counts the coins, not the cents.

sets.title: Make the same amount in different ways

items.q: Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: Each nickel is 5¢. Count by 5¢: 5¢, 10¢. That is 10¢. 1 dime also makes 10¢.

items.q: Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: Each dime is 10¢. Count by 10¢: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢, 40¢, 50¢. That is 50¢. 2 quarters also make 50¢.

items.q: Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: Each quarter is 25¢. Count by 25¢: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢. That is 100¢. 1 loonie also makes 100¢.

items.q: Which makes 35¢?
items.e: 1 quarter and 1 dime make 35¢. 1 quarter and 1 nickel make 30¢. 4 dimes make 40¢. 2 quarters make 50¢.

items.q: Which makes 50¢?
items.e: 2 quarters make 50¢. 1 quarter and 2 dimes make 45¢. 3 dimes make 30¢. 2 quarters and 1 nickel make 55¢.

items.q: Which does not make 60¢?
items.e: 2 quarters and 1 nickel make 55¢, not 60¢. The others all make 60¢.

items.q: Benjamin has 3 coins. They make 45¢. Which coins does he have?
items.e: 1 quarter and 2 dimes make 45¢. 1 quarter, 1 dime and 1 nickel make 40¢. 2 quarters and 1 nickel make 55¢. 3 dimes make 30¢.

items.q: Which makes 75¢?
items.e: 3 quarters make 75¢. 2 quarters and 2 dimes make 70¢. 2 quarters and 1 dime make 60¢. 4 quarters make 100¢.

items.q: Which does not make 100¢?
items.e: 3 quarters and 2 dimes make 95¢, not 100¢. The others all make 100¢.

items.q: Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: Start with the biggest one and count on: 100¢, 125¢, 150¢. That is 150¢. 6 quarters also make 150¢.

items.q: Which makes 120¢?
items.e: 1 loonie and 2 dimes make 120¢. 1 loonie and 2 nickels make 110¢. 1 loonie and 2 quarters make 150¢. 4 quarters and 1 nickel make 105¢.

items.q: Which makes 200¢, the same as a toonie?
items.e: 8 quarters make 200¢. 7 quarters make 175¢. 1 loonie and 2 quarters make 150¢. 1 loonie and 9 dimes make 190¢.

items.q: Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: Each loonie is 100¢. Count by 100¢: 100¢, 200¢. That is 200¢. 1 toonie also makes 200¢.

items.q: Which makes $5?
items.e: 2 toonies and 1 loonie make $5. 2 toonies make $4. 5 toonies make $10. 1 toonie and 1 loonie make $3.

items.q: Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: One $10 bill is $10. 5 toonies also make $10.

items.q: Which makes $20?
items.e: 4 $5 bills make $20. 2 $5 bills make $10. 5 $5 bills make $25. 3 $5 bills make $15.

items.q: Which does not make $50?
items.e: 2 $20 bills and 1 $5 bill make $45, not $50. The others all make $50.

items.q: Which makes $100?
items.e: 5 $20 bills make $100. 4 $20 bills make $80. 1 $50 bill and 1 $20 bill make $70. 10 $5 bills make $50.

items.q: Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: Each $50 bill is $50. Count by $50: $50, $100. That is $100. 1 $100 bill also makes $100.

items.q: Emma has 3 bills. They make $70. Which bills does she have?
items.e: 1 $50 bill and 2 $10 bills make $70. 3 $20 bills make $60. 2 $20 bills and 1 $10 bill make $50. 1 $50 bill, 1 $20 bill and 1 $5 bill make $75.

sets.title: Fewest coins or bills and word problems

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 30¢?
items.e: Use the biggest one you can each time: 1 quarter and 1 nickel make 30¢. That is 2 coins. There is no 30¢ coin. Three dimes work, but 2 coins is fewer.

items.q: Which uses the fewest coins to make 40¢?
items.e: All of these make 40¢. 1 quarter, 1 dime and 1 nickel use only 3 coins. Start with the biggest one you can.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 65¢?
items.e: Use the biggest one you can each time: 2 quarters, 1 dime and 1 nickel make 65¢. That is 4 coins. Three coins can make 60¢ or 75¢, but not 65¢.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 150¢?
items.e: Use the biggest one you can each time: 1 loonie and 2 quarters make 150¢. That is 3 coins. 6 quarters also make 150¢, but that is 6 coins.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make $7?
items.e: Use the biggest one you can each time: 3 toonies and 1 loonie make $7. That is 4 coins. Seven loonies work, but that is 7 coins. Three toonies make only $6.

items.q: Which uses the fewest bills to make $35?
items.e: All of these make $35. 1 $20 bill, 1 $10 bill and 1 $5 bill use only 3 bills. Start with the biggest one you can.

items.q: What is the smallest number of bills you can use to make $80?
items.e: Use the biggest one you can each time: 1 $50 bill, 1 $20 bill and 1 $10 bill make $80. That is 3 bills. 4 $20 bills also make $80, but 3 bills is fewer.

items.q: Leah buys popcorn and a juice box. How much does she spend?
items.e: 35¢ + 50¢: 30¢ + 50¢ = 80¢. 80¢ + 5¢ = 85¢. 15¢ is the difference, not the total.

items.q: Priya has 2 quarters and 1 dime. An apple costs 45¢. Can she buy it?
items.e: Count: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢. Priya has 60¢. 60¢ is more than 45¢. 45¢ + 15¢ = 60¢, so yes, with 15¢ left. 5¢ left comes from counting a quarter as 20¢.

items.q: Ethan has 3 dimes and 2 nickels. A cookie costs 45¢. Can he buy it?
items.e: Dimes: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢. Nickels: 35¢, 40¢. Ethan has 40¢. 40¢ + 5¢ = 45¢, so no, he needs 5¢ more.

items.q: A muffin costs 75¢. Liam has 50¢. How much more does he need?
items.e: Count up from 50¢: 50¢ + 25¢ = 75¢. He needs 25¢ more. 125¢ adds instead of finding the difference.

items.q: For the Terry Fox Run, Amira gives these coins. How much does she give?
items.e: Start with the biggest one and count on: 100¢, 125¢, 150¢, 160¢, 170¢, 180¢. That is 180¢. 6¢ counts the coins. 80¢ forgets that the loonie is 100¢.

items.q: Mateo has 90¢. He buys a pencil for 40¢. How much does he have left?
items.e: Take away: 90¢ − 40¢ = 50¢. Check: 40¢ + 50¢ = 90¢. 130¢ adds instead of taking away.

items.q: Lemonade costs 25¢ a cup. Hana buys 4 cups. How much does she pay?
items.e: Count by 25s: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢. 4 cups cost 100¢, or $1. 80¢ counts a quarter as 20¢.

items.q: At the book fair, a book costs $8 and a poster costs $4. Maya buys both. How much does she spend?
items.e: $8 + $4: $8 + $2 = $10. $10 + $2 = $12. $4 is the difference, not the total.

items.q: Arjun has saved $15. He buys a book for $9. How much money is left?
items.e: Count up from $9: $9 + $1 = $10. $10 + $5 = $15. $1 + $5 = $6. $24 adds instead of taking away.

items.q: A hockey stick costs $35. Nathan has $20. How much more does he need?
Aiden has these coins. A toque costs $8. How much more does he need?
items.e: Toonies: $2, $4. Loonies: $5, $6, $7. Aiden has $7. $7 + $1 = $8, so he needs $1 more. $3 comes from counting each toonie as $1.

items.q: Ava has this money. She pays $10 to rent skates at the rink. How much is left?
items.e: She has $20 + $10 + $5 = $35. Take away $10: $35 − $10 = $25. $45 adds instead of taking away.

items.q: Pizza Day is every Friday. A slice costs $2. Olivia buys a slice every Friday for 4 weeks. How much does she spend?
items.e: $2, $4, $6, $8. 4 slices cost $8. $6 comes from adding 2 + 4.
